title: SIU clears officer who shot hostage-taker
article: A Toronto police sniper had no choice but to shoot dead an armed hostage-taker outside Union Station last month, ending an hourlong rampage witnessed by hundreds of horrified rush-hour commuters, the Special Investigations Unit announced yesterday.

Sugston Anthony Brookes, 45, was felled with a single shot fired by Constable Gordon Lusby, a 15-year veteran of the force. He died after stalking and wounding his estranged wife at a nearby food court, fleeing and then randomly seizing a young woman hostage and holding a sawed-off.22-calibre rifle to her head.
An audiotape examined by the civilian SIU, which investigates all fatal shootings and serious injuries involving police, offered an explanation for Mr. Brookes's actions that day.

On the undated tape, Mr. Brookes "talks about how his estranged wife had wronged him, he makes references to his children, the divorce, and not wanting to go back to jail," SIU spokeswoman Rose Bliss said last night.

On probation for assaulting and threatening his former wife, the gunman also voiced anger at lawyers, social workers, and what he termed "the system." He said, in addition, that he had "made a decision," without specifying what it was.

The Aug. 25 drama, which snarled morning traffic and garnered massive television coverage, began around 8 a. m. when Mr. Brookes confronted his estranged wife, Marlene, in the TD Centre, where she worked at a dry-cleaning plant.
The couple had separated several months earlier when Ms. Brookes moved out, taking the two children with her. Mr. Brookes was subsequently jailed for threatening her with a knife.

After barging into the cleaning plant at around 7 a.m. and demanding to know where his estranged wife was, Mr. Brookes waited for her. As she took the escalator down to the below-ground plant, he fired two or three shots at her, the SIU said.
One grazed her temple and knocked her to the ground. At point-blank range, the gunman then directed his rifle at her head and tried to squeeze off another shot.
But with five rounds still in the chamber, the weapon jammed and Mr. Brookes fled along Wellington Street.
Minutes later, as word of the shooting spread, Mr. Brookes pulled his gun on a police officer who approached him, then hurried toward Front Street. His gun drawn, the officer followed him.

At Union Station, as police descended on the area, Mr. Brookes grabbed pedestrian Nicole Regis, 20. With his left arm around her neck, he held the rifle to her head in a standoff that lasted about 40 minutes.

Ignoring repeated police warnings to drop his gun, Mr. Brookes spent much of that 40 minutes whispering to his terrified captive that he had been wronged by his estranged wife, and telling her he expected to be killed.

He proved correct. At around 8:50, with Emergency Task Force snipers surrounding the pair, Constable Lusby told his supervisor he had a clear, unobstructed line of fire and was ordered to fire his high-powered.308-calibre rifle.
The officer's actions were wholly justified, the SIU concluded.
Ms. Brookes's injuries were not life-threatening and she is recovering from her ordeal. Ms. Regis also escaped without being hurt.
